title: Draws
summary: Not every game has a winner. Learn the ways a game can end in a draw: repetition, the 50-move rule, too little material, and agreement.

steps.title: Half a point each
steps.text: A draw means nobody wins. You already know stalemate. The other ways are: not enough pieces left to checkmate, the same position repeating three times, fifty moves each without a capture or pawn move, and both players agreeing. Here a king and bishop against a lone king can never give checkmate, so the game is drawn at once.
steps.narration: Not every game has a winner. A king and a single bishop can never checkmate a lone king, so this game is already a draw. Let's look at the other ways a game can be drawn.

steps.title: Threefold repetition
steps.text: If the same position appears three times with the same player to move, the game can be claimed as a draw. A player who is losing can use this: checking the king again and again so that it can never escape is called perpetual check. Here White is far behind, and Black threatens checkmate with the queen on c1.
steps.narration: If the exact same position comes up three times, it's a draw. The player who's losing loves this rule. Here White is way behind and about to be mated, but the queen can keep checking forever.

steps.title: Save the game
steps.prompt: You're losing badly. Keep checking the king until the position repeats.
steps.hint: Check from e8. After the king hides on h7, check from h5, and repeat.
steps.success: Black's king can only shuffle between g8 and h7, and your queen keeps checking. The position repeats, and you escape with a draw.
steps.narration: Black has a queen and a rook more, and threatens mate. Don't give up! Check the king, then check it again, back and forth. It can never escape.

steps.title: The 50-move rule
steps.text: If both players make fifty moves each with no capture and no pawn move, either player can claim a draw. This stops a game from dragging on forever when nobody can make progress, like in this ending with a rook each.
steps.narration: There's also the fifty move rule. If fifty moves go by on each side without a capture or a pawn move, the game can be called a draw. Nobody has to shuffle pieces forever.

steps.title: Shaking hands
steps.text: Finally, the players can simply agree to a draw. One offers, the other accepts. In an even position like this pawn ending, where neither side has an advantage, a draw by agreement is common between strong players.
steps.narration: And the simplest draw of all: you both agree. If the position is dead even, one player offers a draw, the other shakes hands, and that's that.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which of these endings is an automatic draw because neither side can ever checkmate?

options.text: King and knight against a lone king
options.why: A single knight with its king cannot force or even reach checkmate, so there is not enough material.

options.text: King and rook against a lone king
options.why: A rook and king can force checkmate. That ending is a win.

options.text: King and pawn against a lone king
options.why: The pawn might promote to a queen, so the game goes on.

steps.narration: Last question, and you've finished the rules of the game! Which of these endings is a dead draw?
